data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution has no conscious goal of error elimination, whereas Popperian science does.","Natural selection acts on reproduction rates, not on the logical content of genetic codes.","Evolutionary fitness is relative to a specific environment, while Popperian corroboration aims at universal logical consistency."],"overturn_conditions":["If it can be shown that 'severity' cannot be assessed without assuming the uniformity of nature.","If practical action is proven to logically require a degree of belief (probability) rather than just a methodological rule."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of stress tests rather than prediction of future success.","Distinction between procedural optimality and outcome certainty.","Rejection of probabilistic weighting in favor of binary survival status."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_004"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we study the organism that survived the harshest winter to understand resilience, not to guarantee it will survive the next one, we choose the best-corroborated theory to test its limits, not to bet on its truth.","The 'fittest' in science is the most falsifiable, not the most adaptable, distinguishing the analogy from standard evolutionary epistemology."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a non-inductive methodological rule to maximize the severity of potential falsification; however, accepting this defense costs the scientist any rational assurance that the chosen theory is likely true or practically reliable, reducing scientific action to a game of 'survival of the boldest' without epistemic probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the goal of science is defined as finding 'likely true' theories rather than 'fast-falsifiable' ones, the Popperian preference becomes indefensible without smuggling in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'severity' itself implicitly assumes that past resistance to falsification correlates with future resistance, the mechanism collapses into circular induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If practical action (e.g., building a bridge) requires a belief in reliability rather than just a willingness to test, the Popperian account fails to guide real-world decisions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which implies increasing probability/truth-likeness via induction) and 'selection criteria' (which are procedural rules for testing). By framing the preference as a rule to subject theories to the hardest possible tests (severity), the choice of the best-corroborated theory is simply the choice of the theory that has survived the most stringent attempts at destruction. This avoids induction because it makes no claim about the future; it only states that if we want to learn fast (falsify errors quickly), we must pick the theory that has already withstood the most severe attacks, as it offers the greatest exposure to future refutation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
